rv.q: At the Irish Rep, director Ciarán O’Reilly has brought O’Neill’s expressionist howl back for a swift, sturdy, smaller-scale revival that now feels unnervingly on-the-pulse.
Otherwise, the production marches rather dully to a foreshadowed conclusion, navigating O'Neill's endlessly indulgent soliloquies along the way.
You’ll have trouble taking your eyes off the actor, or shaking off this fierce, timely staging after the curtain falls.

Through stunning period design, brutally efficient staging, and memorable performances, O’Reilly and company show how this 1922 “comedy of ancient and modern life” is, in fact, an ongoing tragedy in 2026, as the world spins faster and we hang on for dear life.
O’Reilly presents the material truthfully and memorably enough to overcome flaws–even two which might otherwise sink a staging.
For all this expertise and some solid acting, a preview performance the other evening was not as striking as might be expected.
How well does O’Reilly bring O’Neill’s angry (gorilla-like?) opus to the stage? Moderately well.

Ciarán O'Reilly's stylish revival benefits from an evocative set and lighting design that makes the most of the Irish Rep's cramped stage as well as a star-making turn by Jon Beavers ( Paradise ) in the title role.

cn.t: O'Neill's century-old class drama feels timely in this Irish Rep revival, with Jon Beavers delivering a powerful star turn, though critics are divided on whether the expressionistic production fully captures the play's primal intensity.
